Read About Moscow

A city rebuilt on its own foundations again and again — by fire, by revolution, by war, and always regrown around the same red walls.

A Village That Outgrew Every Rival

Moscow's first written mention comes from 1147, a single line in a chronicle noting that Prince Yuri Dolgoruky invited an ally to "come to me, brother, to Moscow" — a minor fortified outpost on the edge of the principality, nothing like the trading power of Novgorod to the north or the political weight of Kyiv to the south. Its rise had nothing to do with geography favoring it and everything to do with a chain of Moscow princes who out-married, out-taxed and outlasted every rival house. By the time Ivan the Terrible was crowned the first Tsar of All Russia in 1547 inside the Kremlin's Dormition Cathedral, Moscow's princes had spent three centuries absorbing neighboring principalities one marriage and one military campaign at a time, and the city that had once bent the knee to Mongol khans was now the seat from which Russia itself would be ruled for the next four hundred years, save one notable interruption.

The City That Stopped Being the Capital

That interruption lasted two centuries. In 1712 Peter the Great, determined to drag Russia toward Europe, moved the capital to a swamp on the Baltic coast he had just conquered from Sweden and named after himself — Saint Petersburg. Moscow kept its cathedrals, its coronations and its symbolic weight — every tsar still traveled south to be crowned in the Kremlin — but the court, the ministries and the money moved north. Napoleon's army found Moscow this way in September 1812: a wealthy but secondary city that its own governor ordered burned to the ground rather than surrender intact, leaving the invading army nothing to winter in and starting its catastrophic retreat. The capital did not return until 1918, when the new Bolshevik government, distrustful of a Petrograd surrounded by hostile fronts and closer to the old imperial court's ghosts, relocated the seat of power back to the Kremlin for the first time in two hundred years.

Almost nothing standing in central Moscow predates the 1930s in its current form — the city was rebuilt, sometimes literally moved, to serve as the stage for a revolution that needed a stage.

Building a Soviet Capital From Scratch

What Stalin inherited in 1918 was a medieval merchant city with narrow lanes never meant for parades or tanks, so he rebuilt it. Tverskaya Street was widened into a formal boulevard; stone apartment blocks too valuable to demolish were jacked onto rails and moved sideways, sometimes with residents still inside; the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, the tallest Orthodox church in the world at the time, was dynamited in 1931 to make way for a planned Palace of Soviets that would have topped the Empire State Building — a project abandoned at the outbreak of war, its foundation left to fill with groundwater and eventually converted into the world's largest open-air swimming pool for three decades. The Moscow Metro, opened in 1935, was built as a matching political statement: stations decorated as "palaces for the people," their marble and mosaics designed so that a factory worker's daily commute passed through rooms more opulent than anything the old aristocracy had built for itself.

Rebuilding Again, After 1991

The Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 triggered a third reconstruction. The swimming pool where the cathedral once stood was drained and the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was rebuilt on the same foundations through the 1990s, an almost exact replica completed in 2000 — a physical undoing of Stalin's most symbolic demolition. Ritz-Carlton towers, glass office blocks and the Moscow-City financial district rose through the 2000s in a city that had spent seventy years building nothing taller than what the Party allowed. Zaryadye Park, opened in 2017 on the site of a demolished Soviet-era hotel next to the Kremlin wall, is the newest chapter in the same pattern: clear the old thing away, build something that says who is in charge now, and let the layers of history stack up underneath.
